text: CHAPTER THREE: DATA FOR MODERN ANALYTICS
Prepared by: Inst. Caesar Gabriel M. Fernando
At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:
Explain Domain III and connect data requirements to the business and analytics problem.
Differentiate traditional data warehouses, data lakes, lakehouses, streaming/event architectures, data mesh, data fabric, and hybrid data-platform patterns according to analytical need.
Explain how batch, streaming, CDC, cloud elasticity, semantic layers, catalogs, lineage, and AI-ready representations affect the feasibility and timeliness of analytics.
Evaluate architecture trade-offs involving latency, scale, variety, governance, interoperability, team ownership, cost, and complexity.
Design a high-level analytics-ready data platform for a realistic application and justify what should remain simple, what should scale, and what should be governed.

text: Domain III begins after the business and analytics problem have been sufficiently framed.

Its responsibility is to determine specific data needs; identify sources, structure, and management approach; acquire and prepare data; harmonize and validate it; and document it so the analytics team can rely on it.
Data findings may force a return to earlier problem framing when assumptions prove wrong or required evidence does not exist.
We do not reduce Domain III to “clean the CSV.” It is the bridge between an analytical question and the data ecosystem that can credibly support it.

text: The Important Shift — Managing Data vs. Applying Analytics
How should enterprise data be governed?
What governance is required for this analytical use?
Which architecture makes this decision possible at the needed latency and scale?
How should evidence be integrated for this analytical question?
Which quality dimensions can invalidate this specific claim?
Where should each workload be served—BI, ML, real-time, geospatial, AI, optimization?
ELE2BA Recall — What Still Matters from Enterprise Data
Definitions must be shared: the same KPI or field cannot mean different things across systems without consequence.
Ownership matters: available data are not automatically authorized data.
Quality is multidimensional: completeness alone does not guarantee usability.
Lineage matters: analytical trust depends on knowing where data came from and what transformed it.
Pipelines matter: repeatable analytics requires repeatable data preparation.

text: Foundations of a Modern Data Platform
A data platform is the integrated set of architectural capabilities that acquire, store, process, govern, orchestrate, and serve data for operational, analytical, and AI use.
A platform is broader than a database and broader than a dashboard.
Its value is not “having many tools.” Its value is making trustworthy data reusable across decisions and workloads.
notes: Modernize the definition by making consumption, governance, orchestration, and ML/AI first-class rather than treating the platform as storage alone.

text: The Modern Data Platform as an Evidence Supply Chain
Analytics and AI turn them into evidence for decisions.
Monitoring keeps the chain reliable over time.
notes: We focus on asking where evidence can fail: delayed ingestion, inconsistent definitions, broken joins, stale gold tables, undocumented transformations, access denial, or an unreachable dashboard.

text: Eight Capabilities of an Analytics-Ready Data Platform
Bring data from databases, files, APIs, devices, partners, and streams
Retain structured, semi-structured, unstructured, and event data appropriately
Clean, standardize, join, aggregate, enrich, and engineer analytical representations
Schedule, coordinate, test, monitor, retry, and trace data workflows
Describe meaning, ownership, lineage, definitions, and business metrics
Control access, policy, retention, acceptable use, and accountability
Deliver data to BI, notebooks, APIs, ML, optimization, operational apps, and AI
Provide scalable compute, reusable environments, feature/vector access, and lifecycle support
Ingestion — Getting Evidence into the Platform
Batch ingestion: periodic files, database extracts, scheduled API pulls.
Streaming/event ingestion: data captured continuously as events occur.
Change Data Capture: propagate source-system inserts, updates, and deletes without reloading everything.
File/object ingestion: CSV, JSON, Parquet, images, audio, documents.
The right ingestion pattern follows decision latency and source behavior.

text: Storage — Not Every Dataset Belongs in the Same Place
Relational stores are strong for structured transactions and integrity.
Analytical warehouses are strong for curated, query-oriented structured analytics.
Object storage/data lakes are strong for scalable heterogeneous data and open file formats.
Lakehouses add table-management and analytical capabilities over low-cost data-lake storage.
Specialized stores may serve time-series, graph, search, geospatial, or vector workloads.

text: Orchestration and Observability — The Platform Must Know When It Breaks
Orchestration coordinates dependencies, schedules, retries, and workflow order.
Observability detects stale data, schema changes, failed jobs, volume anomalies, and latency problems.
A dashboard can be visually correct while its source pipeline silently failed yesterday.
Operational trust requires monitoring the data pipeline, not only the final model.

text: Governance and Security Are Cross-Cutting Fabrics
Governance does not sit at the end of the pipeline; it applies across source, ingestion, storage, processing, serving, and lifecycle.
Controls may include identity/access management, encryption, classification, retention, lineage, policy, data minimization, audit, and approved purpose.
Modern distributed platforms increase—not decrease—the need for coherent governance.

text: ML and AI Enablement: A Modern Platform Serves More Than BI
Traditional BI primarily consumes curated historical measures.
Machine learning may require large training datasets, feature histories, labels, reproducible snapshots, and low-latency scoring inputs.
Generative/semantic applications may require documents, metadata, embeddings, retrieval indexes, and access controls.
The platform must support these workloads without allowing AI experimentation to bypass governance.

text: Big Data: The Workload Changed Before the Buzzword Did
NIST describes Big Data in terms of extensive data whose characteristics can overwhelm traditional technical approaches.
ISO/IEC 20546 provides standardized terminology and a conceptual overview for Big Data.
The practical lesson: Big Data is not simply “many rows.” It is a workload whose scale, speed, heterogeneity, or complexity changes the architecture required to process it.

text: Volume: The sheer scale and massive amount of data generated.
Velocity: The high speed at which data accumulates and needs to be processed.
Variety: The diverse formats (structured and unstructured) from various sources.
Veracity: The accuracy, quality, and trustworthiness of the data.
Value: The actionable and useful insights

alt_text.name: Picture 3

text: The amount of data generated, collected, and stored. Volume becomes a challenge when the scale strains the tools used to manage or analyze it; there is no universal size threshold for “big.”
A grocery chain accumulates millions of POS transaction lines across its branches and years of operation.
The rate at which data arrives, together with the speed at which it must be processed and used. The question is whether information can be acted on while it is still relevant.
If Wondermart receives stock alerts throughout the day, staff need to see them soon enough to replenish shelves before a stockout continues.
The diversity of data sources, structures, and formats, including structured tables, semi-structured files, and unstructured material.
Wondermart combines POS records in CSV, inventory in a spreadsheet, promotions in JSON, and customer feedback in XML.
The extent to which data can be trusted for an analysis. Accuracy, completeness, consistency, source reliability, and uncertainty affect the conclusions it can support.
A customer complaint identifies a store and category but no SKU. It cannot reliably be attributed to one specific product.
The useful benefit gained when data is analyzed and applied to a question or decision. Collecting more data alone does not establish value.
Wondermart uses validated sales and stockout evidence to choose replenishment priorities for its next operating cycle.

text: Veracity and Value — Useful Extensions, Not Magic Words
Veracity asks whether the data are trustworthy enough for the intended use.
Value asks whether the data and platform improve a meaningful analytical or organizational outcome.
A high-volume stream with poor timestamps may be less useful than a smaller, trustworthy dataset.
A technically impressive platform that does not improve a decision is architecture without analytical value.

text: Latency is the delay between an event occurring and useful evidence becoming available to a decision process.
The required latency should be derived from the decision—not from a desire to label everything “real-time.”
Monthly budgeting may tolerate hours or days; fraud screening, equipment protection, or flood-response alerts may require seconds or minutes.

text: Data are accumulated and processed on a schedule or in bounded jobs.
Strengths: simpler operations, efficient large-scale processing, easier reproducibility for many historical workloads.
Examples: nightly KPI refresh, monthly financial close, semester analytics, weekly model retraining.
Batch is not “old.” It remains the correct architecture when decision latency does not require continuous processing.

They support continuous monitoring, low-latency aggregation, alerting, and event-driven decision systems.
Examples: fraud events, sensors, clicks, GPS, equipment telemetry, market feeds, network monitoring.

text: Event Time vs. Processing TimeWhy “When” is harder then it looks
Event time: when the real-world event actually happened.
Processing time: when the platform received or processed it.
Late, duplicated, or out-of-order events can distort real-time aggregates.
For sensor and mobility analytics, time semantics are part of data quality and analytical validity.

text: CDC captures database changes—such as inserts, updates, and deletes—and propagates them downstream.
Instead of re-extracting an entire table, the analytical platform can process what changed.
CDC is useful for fresher analytics, operational synchronization, and event-driven architectures.
It also creates governance and ordering concerns: downstream systems must understand change semantics.

text: A data warehouse organizes integrated, curated data for analytical querying, reporting, and decision support. Strengths include mature SQL analytics, dimensional modeling, governed metrics, and predictable BI performance. Limitations emerge when organizations need inexpensive storage of diverse raw data, large-scale data science, streaming, or non-tabular workloads.

A data lake retains large volumes of data—often in open or flexible formats—before all downstream uses are known. It supports structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data, exploratory analytics, and data science. Without strong metadata, governance, quality, and table-management practices, a lake can become difficult to trust and navigate.

text: Organizations often stored raw/diverse data in a lake, then copied selected data into a warehouse for BI.
This pattern can create duplicated data, multiple definitions, staleness, extra pipelines, and separate governance surfaces.
The lakehouse idea emerged partly to reduce the gap between low-cost open storage and warehouse-like management/performance.

text: Armbrust et al. describe the lakehouse as an architecture built on open, directly accessible data formats while adding data-management capabilities traditionally associated with analytical DBMSs.
The intended convergence includes BI, data science, and machine learning over a more unified data foundation.
Key enabling ideas include transaction management, metadata, versioning, indexing/optimization, and open columnar formats.

text: Open columnar file formats such as Parquet allow multiple analytical engines to read the same underlying data.
Modern table formats/layers such as Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Apache Hudi add table metadata and management capabilities over object storage.
The architectural objective is interoperability and reliable table behavior—not allegiance to a single engine.

text: Preserve source data close to original form
Raw sensor events, raw GPS, raw hotline payloads
Standard road IDs, cleaned sensor units, matched locations
Road-risk table, barangay disruption KPI, model-ready feature set
The labels are optional; the principle is what matters: preserve raw evidence, create reusable validated data, then publish purpose-built analytical products.
A small project may need only source → validated → analytical output.
A large platform may need many domains, quality zones, sandboxes, or serving layers. Architecture should be as simple as the decision allows and as robust as the risk requires.
ETL: Extract → Transform → Load. Transformation occurs before data reach the main analytical destination.
ELT: Extract → Load → Transform. Raw or lightly processed data are loaded first, then transformed using scalable analytical-platform compute.
Cloud object storage and scalable compute made ELT attractive for many modern analytical workloads.
ETL remains valid when transformations, compliance, bandwidth, or target constraints require it.

text: Cloud-Native Analytics — Why the Architecture Changed
Elastic infrastructure reduces the need to size every system for permanent peak capacity.
Managed services can reduce operational overhead for storage, compute, integration, streaming, and analytics.
Object storage enables inexpensive durable data retention at scale.
Cloud APIs make it easier to compose specialized services—but can also create cost, governance, and lock-in risks.

text: Traditional systems often tied storage capacity and processing capacity together.
Modern cloud/lakehouse architectures frequently allow compute to scale independently from durable storage.
Benefits can include workload isolation, elastic scaling, and multiple engines over shared data.
Trade-offs include data movement, cost control, caching, concurrency, and governance complexity.

text: Serverless means infrastructure provisioning and scaling are substantially abstracted from the user.
Teams focus more on jobs, queries, functions, or pipelines and less on managing individual servers.
Benefits: elasticity and reduced operations for suitable workloads.
Risks: unpredictable cost, service limits, cold starts, portability concerns, and reduced low-level control.

text: Centralized, Decentralized, and Hybrid Data Architectures
A centralized platform concentrates data engineering, governance, infrastructure, and analytical serving into a common organizational environment.
Strengths: consistency, shared standards, centralized expertise, easier control.
Risks: bottlenecks, distance from domain meaning, slow response to many competing teams.

text: Data mesh is a socio-technical approach for scaling data ownership across domains.
Its four widely cited principles are domain-oriented decentralized data ownership, data as a product, self-service data infrastructure, and federated computational governance.
The core problem it addresses is not only storage scale, but organizational scale: too many domains, sources, users, and changes for one central team to mediate efficiently.

text: A data product is designed for consumers, not merely emitted as a by-product of an operational system.
Useful properties include clear ownership, discoverability, documented semantics, quality expectations, reliable interfaces, security, and lifecycle responsibility.
Examples: “Road Accessibility by Segment” or “Validated Rainfall Event Feed” rather than “table_2026_final_v3.”

text: Data Fabric — Unifying Access Through Metadata and Automation

Recent literature describes data fabric as a metadata- and automation-oriented approach that connects heterogeneous data across distributed environments while maintaining unified access and governance.
It often emphasizes metadata, semantic relationships, automation, integration, and policy across on-premises, cloud, and edge sources.
Unlike data mesh, fabric is primarily an integration/technology architecture rather than an organizational ownership model.

text: Hybrid and Federated Models — What Most Organizations Actually Look Like
Real organizations often combine centralized platform services with decentralized domain ownership.
Shared teams may operate identity, catalogs, compute, observability, and security while domains own data products and business semantics.
The design problem is balancing local autonomy with enterprise consistency.
Working industry concept: a data contract makes expectations between data producers and consumers explicit.
It may specify schema, semantics, quality rules, freshness, ownership, compatibility, and change expectations.
The goal is to reduce silent breakage when upstream systems evolve.
Treat data contracts as an emerging industry practice—not a universal standard.

text: Catalogs, Metadata, and Lineage:Find It, Understand It, Trust It
Catalog: helps users discover available data assets and their metadata.
Metadata: describes meaning, owner, structure, sensitivity, quality, and operational properties.
Lineage: traces how data move and transform from sources to analytical outputs.
Together they reduce the “tribal knowledge” problem of modern data platforms.
Semantic / Metrics Layer — One KPI, One Meaning
A semantic layer translates physical data structures into shared business concepts, relationships, dimensions, and measures.
A metrics layer centralizes reusable metric definitions so “SLA Compliance,” “Active Student,” or “Gross Margin” are not recalculated differently in every dashboard.
This is the data-platform counterpart of Chapter 2 KPI discipline.

text: Modern Analytical Data Is More Than Tables
Multimodal Analytics — When Evidence Comes in Different Forms
A multimodal analytical problem combines evidence from more than one data modality.
A flood monitoring analytics system might combine a citizen text report, photo, GPS coordinate, rainfall sensor reading, and road-network data.
The challenge is not merely storing files; it is aligning identity, time, place, meaning, permissions, and confidence across modalities.

text: May also include large unstructured corpora and multimodal assets
May require labels, embeddings, feature histories, prompt/retrieval context
Fit for training, inference, retrieval, or agentic use
Requires the same—plus stronger attention to provenance, rights, bias, drift, and reuse risk
AI-ready should never imply “remove governance to move faster.” Modern AI increases the importance of data provenance, permissions, quality, and context.
Applying Modern Data Platforms Across Industries
There Is No Universal “Best” Modern Data Architecture
Warehouse, lakehouse, mesh, fabric, streaming, serverless, and vector technologies solve different problems.
A good architecture is proportionate to the analytical need, organizational scale, risk, latency, skills, and budget.
Over-architecture creates cost and operational burden; under-architecture creates bottlenecks and unreliable evidence.
How fast must the decision happen?
How much and what kinds of data?
How stable are schemas and sources?
BI, ML, geospatial, APIs, vector retrieval
What skills and operating capacity exist?
What failure can the organization tolerate?
Modern Trends Worth Watching — and Why
Process data closer to devices when latency/connectivity matter
Learn across distributed data without centralizing everything
Structured cross-organization data exchange and control
AI assists metadata, testing, transformation, discovery, monitoring
Human accountability and correctness remain necessary
Domain III is not “just cleaning.” It translates analytical evidence needs into a trustworthy data plan.
Analytics Application uses prior data-management knowledge to justify architecture for specific decisions.
Big Data is a workload problem. Volume, velocity, variety, variability, and latency can force different systems choices.
Modern architecture is plural. Warehouses, lakes, lakehouses, streaming, mesh, fabric, and specialized stores solve different problems.
Real-time is a requirement, not a status symbol. Use it only when delayed evidence loses decision value.
AI-ready data still require governance. Metadata, lineage, quality, rights, representativeness, and monitoring become more—not less—important.
The best architecture is the simplest defensible architecture that delivers the right evidence to the right decision at the right time.
